papers.title: Off-target myocardial necrosis due to incomplete balloon occlusion during retrograde coronary venous ethanol ablation.
papers.authors: Zhang HD, Ding L, Liu YD, Qi YJ, Zhang K, Jiang ZH, et al.
papers.citation: Zhang HD, Ding L, Liu YD, Qi YJ, Zhang K, Jiang ZH, et al.. Off-target myocardial necrosis due to incomplete balloon occlusion during retrograde coronary venous ethanol ablation.. Heart Rhythm. 2026 Nov 15;23(11):e3016-e3028. doi: 10.1016/j.hrthm.2026.05.022 doi.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND:
It is assumed that complete balloon occlusion is necessary for effective lesion formation in retrograde coronary venous ethanol infusion for ventricular arrhythmias.

OBJECTIVE:
This study aimed to evaluate the myocardial effects of ethanol infusion under conditions of incomplete balloon occlusion.

METHODS:
12 swine were randomized into acute (n = 6) and chronic (n = 6) cohorts. Ethanol was infused into different coronary veins using single over-the-wire balloons sized to achieve incomplete occlusion. Myocardial injury was assessed by gross pathology, histology, and ultrastructural analysis.

RESULTS:
Incomplete balloon occlusion was confirmed in all animals, with distal venous leakage in 9 of 12 and collateral filling in 3 of 12. Myocardial staining was observed in only 4 of 12, faint and poorly localized. Despite this, all acute animals developed lesions, with transmural infarction in 5 of 6. Gross lesion dimensions reached up to 30 mm in width, 86 mm in length, and 15.0 mm in depth. Acute histology revealed eosinophilic changes, vacuolar degeneration, and cardiomyocyte necrosis. Ultrastructural analysis demonstrated plasma membrane rupture, sarcomeric dissolution, mitochondrial swelling, and intercalated disk disruption. In the chronic phase, 4 of 6 swine presented with transmural fibrotic scars (up to 46 mm wide, 58 mm long, and 14.8 mm deep), characterized by replacement fibrosis, myocyte atrophy, and inflammation. Chronic ultrastructural changes included mitochondrial degeneration, intercalated disk remodeling, sarcomere disorganization, and vacuolar pathology.

CONCLUSION:
Incomplete balloon occlusion during retrograde coronary venous ethanol infusion can still produce large, transmural infarctions. These findings underscore the potential for off-target necrosis and the need for precise procedural control in ethanol ablation for ventricular arrhythmias.
papers.titleJa: 逆行性冠静脈エタノールアブレーション中のバルーンの不完全閉塞によるオフターゲット心筋壊死。

この研究はevを目的とした（観察研究・その他 / N = 6例）

It is assumed that complete balloon occlusion is necessary for effective lesion formation in retrograde coronary venous ethanol infusion for ventricular arrhythmias.

【目的】

This study aimed to evaluate the myocardial effects of ethanol infusion under conditions of incomplete balloon occlusion.

METHODS:
12 swine were randomized into acute (n = 6) and chronic (n = 6) cohorts.  Ethanol was infused into different coronary veins using single over-the-wire balloons sized to achieve incomplete occlusion.
Myocardial injury was assessed by gross pathology, histology, and ultrastructural analysis.

RESULTS:
Incomplete balloon occlusion was confirmed in all animals, with distal venous leakage in 9 of 12 and collateral filling in 3 of 12.  Myocardial staining was observed in only 4 of 12, faint and poorly localized.  Despite this, all acute animals developed lesions, with transmural infarction in 5 of 6.  Gross lesion dimensions reached up to 30 mm in width, 86 mm in length, and 15.0 mm in depth.  Acute histology revealed eosinophilic changes, vacuolar degeneration, and cardiomyocyte necrosis.
Ultrastructural analysis demonstrated plasma membrane rupture, sarcomeric dissolution, mitochondrial swelling, and intercalated disk disruption.  In the chronic phase, 4 of 6 swine presented with transmural fibrotic scars (up to 46 mm wide, 58 mm long, and 14.8 mm deep), characterized by replacement fibrosis, myocyte atrophy, and inflammation.
Chronic ultrastructural changes included mitochondrial degeneration, intercalated disk remodeling, sarcomere disorganization, and vacuolar pathology.

CONCLUSION:
Incomplete balloon occlusion during retrograde coronary venous ethanol infusion can still produce large, transmural infarctions.  These findings underscore the potential for off-target necrosis and the need for precise procedural control in ethanol ablation for ventricular arrhythmias.

papers.title: Microbubble and thermal profile of an eight-spline pulsed field ablation system in a pre-clinical model.
papers.journal: Journal of interventional cardiac electrophysiology : an international journal of arrhythmias and pacing
papers.authors: Niemiera B, Ranjan R, Piccini JP, Nguyen J, Mittal L, Pipenhagen C, et al.
papers.citation: Niemiera B, Ranjan R, Piccini JP, Nguyen J, Mittal L, Pipenhagen C, et al.. Microbubble and thermal profile of an eight-spline pulsed field ablation system in a pre-clinical model.. J Interv Card Electrophysiol. 2026 Aug 16;69(5):1011-1023. doi: 10.1007/s10840-025-02145-1 doi.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND:
Pulsed field ablation (PFA) has become a clinically accepted energy modality for catheter ablation of atrial fibrillation. As PFA catheters improve and evolve, iatrogenic cerebral events remain an important consideration when evaluating the safety of new devices. Several factors unique to each PFA system have the potential to lead to embolic events, including but not limited to thermal effects leading to char or coagulum formation and microbubble production.

OBJECTIVES:
To characterize the thermal profile and microbubble production from an 8-spline balloon-in-basket PFA catheter.

METHODS:
PFA applications from a 12.5 F, over-the-wire, balloon-in-basket PFA catheter were performed on non-perfused ex vivo bovine tissue. Fiber-optic thermometry probes were used to assess temperature (surface, 3 mm, and 7 mm intramurally) after 8, 16, and 70 consecutive PFA applications. Gross and histopathological assessments were completed to assess for indicators of thermal tissue damage. Microbubble production was evaluated using an extracorporeal blood loop (left femoral vein and right femoral artery loop in N = 6 swine) with an ultrasonic bubble counter and flow meter. For each application, microbubble quantity, size, and gas volume were measured.

RESULTS:
None of the ablations resulted in a tissue temperature above 50 °C. A single ablation produced, on average, 187 microbubbles and 30.3 nL of gas. The PFA system produced bubbles with an average diameter of 43 µm. All measures were significantly below the RF derived thresholds of 1174 microbubbles, 1128 nL, and 49 µm, respectively.

CONCLUSION:
This 12.5 F, over-the-wire, balloon-in-basket PFA catheter and associated therapy did not lead to clinically significant temperature rises that may cause thermal necrosis, char, and coagulum. In addition, this PFA catheter produced fewer and smaller microbubbles with less total gas volume compared to radiofrequency (RF) devices with available data.

papers.title: Stroke risk-based anticoagulation after atrial fibrillation ablation: ALONE-AF post hoc analysis.
papers.authors: Lee YS, Uhm JS, Park J, Kim D, Yang PS, Yu HT, et al.
papers.citation: Lee YS, Uhm JS, Park J, Kim D, Yang PS, Yu HT, et al.. Stroke risk-based anticoagulation after atrial fibrillation ablation: ALONE-AF post hoc analysis.. Heart Rhythm. 2026 Oct 16;:. doi: 10.1016/j.hrthm.2026.10.009 doi.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND:
Discontinuation of oral anticoagulant (OAC) in patients without recurrent atrial arrhythmia after ablation for atrial fibrillation (AF) has been demonstrated to reduce composite outcomes of stroke, systemic embolism, and major bleeding compared with continued OAC.

OBJECTIVE:
This study aimed to evaluate the optimal OAC strategy according to baseline stroke risk and AF recurrence.

METHODS:
In this post hoc analysis of the long-term anticoagulation discontinuation after catheter ablation for AF (ALONE-AF) trial, patients were stratified according to CHADS-VASc score of ≤2 and ≥3. Within each stratum, outcomes were compared between the OAC discontinuation and continuation subgroups. The cumulative incidence of stroke, systemic embolism, and major bleeding at 2 years was estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method, with competing risk analysis accounting for AF recurrence.

RESULTS:
Among 840 patients, 584 and 256 had a CHADS-VASc score ≤2 (mean age 62.0 ±7.5 years, 15.9% female) and ≥3 (mean age 68.9 ±7.3 years, 45.3% female), respectively. In the CHADS-VASc ≤2 stratum, the primary outcome occurred in 1 patient (0.4%) in the discontinuation subgroup vs 6 (2.4%) in the continuation subgroup (absolute difference -1.9 percentage points, P = .066). In the CHADS-VASc ≥3 stratum, 2 events (1.8%) occurred in the continuation subgroup only (absolute difference -1.8 percentage points, P = .172). All major bleeding events (n = 5) occurred in the continuation subgroups. Competing risk analysis yielded consistent results.

CONCLUSIONS:
In this exploratory post hoc analysis, no statistically significant differences in outcomes were observed between OAC strategies when stratified by CHADS-VASc score, though event numbers were limited. Larger prospective trials are needed to confirm these observations.

papers.title: Integrated hemodynamic sensing, electrical sensing, and ventricular pacing from a novel substernal lead: An acute human study.
papers.authors: Cai C, Gu K, Gaskill B, Ding X, Li Y, Chen M
papers.citation: Cai C, Gu K, Gaskill B, Ding X, Li Y, Chen M. Integrated hemodynamic sensing, electrical sensing, and ventricular pacing from a novel substernal lead: An acute human study.. Heart Rhythm. 2026 Sep 20;:. doi: 10.1016/j.hrthm.2026.08.047 doi.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND:
Implantable cardioverter defibrillators rely primarily on electrical signals to guide therapy. Hemodynamic sensing may provide complementary information about the immediate physiological consequences of arrhythmias.

OBJECTIVE:
In this study, we evaluated the acute feasibility and performance of a 3-dimensional substernal shock lead that integrates hemodynamic sensing, electrical sensing, and ventricular pacing.

METHODS:
This prospective first-in-human feasibility study enrolled 5 patients undergoing cardiac surgery or epicardial ventricular tachycardia (VT) ablation. A substernal shock lead was temporarily placed through a percutaneous subxiphoid approach using a dedicated delivery system. Lead placement and removal, adverse events, synchronized sensor signals, surface electrocardiograms, substernal electrograms, and pacing thresholds were assessed.

RESULTS:
Lead placement and removal were successful in all patients without device- or procedure-related acute adverse events. Interpretable hemodynamic signals were obtained in all 5 patients and showed stable beat-to-beat temporal correspondence with the electrocardiogram and distinct rhythm-associated patterns across sinus rhythm, atrial fibrillation, VT, and ventricular fibrillation. All 147 VT episodes had interpretable hemodynamic-index recordings. The hemodynamic index decreased abruptly during VT and recovered after arrhythmia termination. Corresponding changes in the hemodynamic index were observed during transitions among VT, ventricular fibrillation, and sinus rhythm. Ventricular capture was achieved in all 5 patients at 11-17 V (mean, 13.8 V) at 0.5 ms.

CONCLUSION:
Acute placement of this multifunctional substernal lead was feasible and enabled integrated hemodynamic and electrical sensing with acute ventricular capture. These findings provide preliminary human support for further development of physiology-guided extravascular implantable cardioverter defibrillator systems; chronic performance and clinical validation of the hemodynamic sensing algorithm require further study.

papers.title: Mechanisms of Recurrent Arrhythmia in Patients With Prior Surgical Ablation of Atrial Fibrillation Who Undergo Catheter Ablation.
papers.authors: Brahier MS, Brahier EA, Schwennesen H, Arps K, Williams A, Zwischenberger B, et al.
papers.citation: Brahier MS, Brahier EA, Schwennesen H, Arps K, Williams A, Zwischenberger B, et al.. Mechanisms of Recurrent Arrhythmia in Patients With Prior Surgical Ablation of Atrial Fibrillation Who Undergo Catheter Ablation.. J Cardiovasc Electrophysiol. 2026 Sep 20;37(9):2047-2054. doi: 10.1111/jce.70477 doi.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND:
Atrial tachyarrhythmias frequently recur after surgical ablation and often require catheter ablation (CA).

METHODS:
We conducted a retrospective cohort study of patients who underwent CA for symptomatic atrial fibrillation or flutter (AF hereafter) following surgical ablation. Clinical data, including patient and surgical characteristics and results of electrophysiology testing and mapping, were recorded. Recurrence was defined as 30 s of AF, atrial flutter, or atrial tachycardia following a 3-month blanking period.

RESULTS:
Thirty-seven patients were included in the study (mean age 67.0 ± 9.8 years, 43% female) who underwent isolated surgical ablation (n = 5), concomitant mitral valve surgery (n = 21), aortic valve (n = 5), tricuspid valve surgery (n = 6), and/or coronary artery bypass grafting (n = 6). The mean time from surgical ablation to CA was 5.9 ± 5.1 years. Among the 37 patients, 19 (51%) experienced one or more pulmonary vein reconnections (mean 3.0 ± 1.3 veins per patient), and 15 (41%) developed mitral annular flutter. Following ablation, 12 (32%) patients developed recurrent arrhythmia by 1-year post-ablation. Age, sex, body mass index, time from surgical ablation to CA left ventricular ejection fraction < 50%, prior CA, left atrial diameter, and mitral annular flutter were not associated with recurrence. The number of pulmonary vein reconnections at the time of repeat CA was predictive of arrhythmia recurrence in subsequent follow-up (OR 2.148 [95% CI: 1.059-4.357]; p = 0.034).

CONCLUSIONS:
Pulmonary vein reconnection and mitral annular flutter are common recurrence mechanisms in patients with symptomatic arrhythmia recurrence following surgical ablation. The number of pulmonary vein reconnections predicts recurrent arrhythmia.

papers.title: Terminal S Wave Pattern in Lead V3 as a Simple Marker for Ventricular Tachycardia Risk Stratification in Patients With Repaired Tetralogy of Fallot.
papers.authors: Matsuoka Y, Igarashi M, Kawamatsu N, Iioka Y, Harano Y, Komatsu Y, et al.
papers.citation: Matsuoka Y, Igarashi M, Kawamatsu N, Iioka Y, Harano Y, Komatsu Y, et al.. Terminal S Wave Pattern in Lead V3 as a Simple Marker for Ventricular Tachycardia Risk Stratification in Patients With Repaired Tetralogy of Fallot.. J Cardiovasc Electrophysiol. 2026 Oct 10;37(10):2261-2269. doi: 10.1111/jce.70468 doi.
papers.abstract:
INTRODUCTION:
Patients with repaired tetralogy of Fallot (rTOF) remain at risk of ventricular tachycardia (VT). This risk is most commonly related to slow conduction within the septal isthmus, which is defined as the region between the ventricular septal defect (VSD) patch and adjacent valvular annuli. While assessment of septal isthmus conduction currently requires invasive electrophysiological mapping, the 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) may offer a noninvasive alternative. Therefore, the present study aimed to identify ECG markers reflecting septal isthmus conduction properties and evaluate their ability to predict isthmus conduction characteristics and VT inducibility.

METHODS AND RESULTS:
In five patients with rTOF undergoing septal isthmus ablation, 12-lead ECGs obtained before and after ablation were compared to identify candidate ECG markers. The identified marker was validated in an independent cohort of 23 patients stratified according to septal isthmus conduction properties into normal conduction (Normal, n = 5), slow-conducting isthmus (SCI, n = 10), and conduction block (Block, n = 8) groups. The results indicated that the terminal S wave (TSW) in lead V3 became more prominent after ablation compared with that before ablation. In the validation cohort, V3 TSW was categorized as absent, small (< 0.1 mV), or large (≥ 0.1 mV), and the TSW patterns differed significantly among the groups (p < 0.001). Specifically, absent TSW was dominant in the Normal group (4/5, 80%), small TSW was the most frequent in the SCI group (7/10, 70%), and large TSW was predominant in the Block group (7/8, 87.5%). Small TSW predicted SCI with 70% sensitivity and 85% specificity (p = 0.013), whereas large TSW predicted Block with 88% sensitivity and 80% specificity (p = 0.006). Moreover, large TSW predicted VT non-inducibility with high specificity and high positive predictive value (p = 0.019).

CONCLUSION:
This study indicates that V3 TSW is a simple, noninvasive ECG marker reflecting septal isthmus conduction properties in rTOF, suggesting its potential utility for VT risk stratification.

papers.title: Impact of application repetition on Joule heating and lesion formation using a circular-shaped pulsed field catheter.
papers.journal: Journal of interventional cardiac electrophysiology : an international journal of arrhythmias and pacing
papers.authors: Okumura M, Yamagami S, Akiyama M, Nakano Y, Amano Y, Okuda T, et al.
papers.citation: Okumura M, Yamagami S, Akiyama M, Nakano Y, Amano Y, Okuda T, et al.. Impact of application repetition on Joule heating and lesion formation using a circular-shaped pulsed field catheter.. J Interv Card Electrophysiol. 2026 Oct 23;69(7):1563-1566. doi: 10.1007/s10840-026-02379-7 doi.
papers.abstract:
INTRODUCTION:
Pulsed field ablation (PFA) is a non-thermal ablation modality, but repeated high-voltage applications can still cause Joule heating at the electrode-tissue interface. We evaluated the effects of application repetition and inter-application intervals on temperature rise and lesion depth using a circular-shaped PFA catheter.

METHODS AND RESULTS:
In an in vitro potato model, a circular-shaped PFA catheter was tested under five settings: 1×, 2×, 2× with a 10-s interval, 4×, and 4× with a 10-s interval. Maximum electrode surface temperature was measured using a thermal camera, and lesion depth was assessed by TTC staining (n = 5 per setting). Temperature increased significantly with application repetition and was attenuated by a 10-s interval (overall P < 0.0001). Lesion depth also increased with repetition (overall P < 0.0001), but did not differ significantly between interval and no-interval conditions at equal application numbers.

CONCLUSION:
In this simplified in vitro model, a short inter-application interval was associated with attenuation of temperature rise during repeated PFA delivery, while lesion depth was not significantly reduced.
papers.titleJa: 円形パルスフィールドカテーテルを使用したジュール加熱と病変形成に対する適用の繰り返しの影響。

papers.abstractJa:
INTRODUCTION:
Pulsed field ablation (PFA) is a non-thermal ablation modality, but repeated high-voltage applications can still cause Joule heating at the electrode-tissue interface.  We evaluated the effects of application repetition and inter-application intervals on temperature rise and lesion depth using a circular-shaped PFA catheter.

METHODS AND RESULTS:
In an in vitro potato model, a circular-shaped PFA catheter was tested under five settings: 1×, 2×, 2× with a 10-s interval, 4×, and 4× with a 10-s interval.
Maximum electrode surface temperature was measured using a thermal camera, and lesion depth was assessed by TTC staining (n = 5 per setting).  Temperature increased significantly with application repetition and was attenuated by a 10-s interval (overall P < 0.0001).
Lesion depth also increased with repetition (overall P < 0.0001), but did not differ significantly between interval and no-interval conditions at equal application numbers.

CONCLUSION:
In this simplified in vitro model, a short inter-application interval was associated with attenuation of temperature rise during repeated PFA delivery, while lesion depth was not significantly reduced.

papers.title: Lattice-tip catheter for septal ventricular tachycardia ablation guided by preprocedural imaging.
papers.authors: Verhaeghe L, Ditac G, Johner N, Tétreault-Langlois M, Sdiri-Cheniti S, Plant A, et al.
papers.citation: Verhaeghe L, Ditac G, Johner N, Tétreault-Langlois M, Sdiri-Cheniti S, Plant A, et al.. Lattice-tip catheter for septal ventricular tachycardia ablation guided by preprocedural imaging.. Heart Rhythm. 2026 Nov 14;23(11):e2864-e2875. doi: 10.1016/j.hrthm.2026.05.008 doi.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND:
Outcomes after ventricular tachycardia (VT) ablation in patients with a septal substrate are poor.

OBJECTIVE:
This study aimed to evaluate a strategy for septal VT ablation combining substrate imaging and a large-footprint dual-energy catheter.

METHODS:
Patients presenting with drug-refractory VT in the setting of a predominantly septal substrate identified on preoperative imaging were prospectively included. Ablation targets were identified through a combination of imaging-based substrate identification and conventional endocardial mapping data. They were targeted using a large-footprint dual-energy catheter.

RESULTS:
12 procedures were performed in 10 consecutive patients. 9 of them had at least 1 previous failed ablation procedure, including nonstandard radiofrequency (RF) ablation strategies in 5. 6 of them were in a VT storm at the time of ablation. Substrate imaging using a computed tomography scan with late iodine acquisition showed intramural septal substrate in all. Noninducibility was reached in 83% of the procedures. 60% remained free from VT after the last procedure with a mean follow-up time of 9.9 ± 2.2 months. The ablation protocol was adapted during the study. In the last 5 patients, where the final optimized ablation protocol was used combining pulsed field and RF energy, 80% remained free from VT.

CONCLUSION:
Septal VT ablation using a strategy combining substrate imaging and large-footprint dual-energy lattice-tip catheter leads to a high rate of noninducibility and good outcomes during short-term follow-up, especially when combining RF and pulsed field energy.

papers.title: Ventricular Fibrillation During Pulsed Field Ablation With Dual-Energy Focal Catheters in Patients With Cardiac Implantable Electronic Devices.
papers.authors: Kong NW, Gamarra N, Kelly FA, Garcia DV, Alhassan H, Locke A, et al.
papers.citation: Kong NW, Gamarra N, Kelly FA, Garcia DV, Alhassan H, Locke A, et al.. Ventricular Fibrillation During Pulsed Field Ablation With Dual-Energy Focal Catheters in Patients With Cardiac Implantable Electronic Devices.. Heart Rhythm. 2026 Nov 06;:. doi: 10.1016/j.hrthm.2026.11.004 doi.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND:
Arrhythmia induction during catheter ablation in patients with cardiac implantable electronic devices (CIEDs) has been reported, but the risk associated with pulsed field ablation (PFA) remains poorly characterized.

OBJECTIVE:
To estimate the procedural incidence of unexpected ventricular fibrillation (VF) during PFA in patients with CIEDs and describe associated clinical and device findings.

METHODS:
We performed a retrospective single-center cohort study of consecutive PFA procedures in patients with CIEDs. All procedures were reviewed for unexpected VF.

RESULTS:
Among 107 consecutive procedures using PFA energy in patients with CIEDs, 83 were atrial and 24 were ventricular ablations. Unexpected VF occurred in 4 patients (overall incidence 3.7%, 95% CI 1.0% - 9.3%): 1 during left atrial PFA for pulmonary vein isolation and 3 during left ventricular PFA for ventricular tachycardia ablations. VF occurred at ablation sites both near and remote from CIED lead tips. Device electrograms demonstrated prominent ablation artifact with abnormal triggered activity and mode switch behavior. Intra-procedural recordings also demonstrated local capture and R on T mechanisms.

CONCLUSIONS:
Unexpected VF during PFA in patients with CIEDs occurred in 3.7% of procedures. These results complement prior adverse-event reports and support systematic pre-, intra-, and post-procedure CIED management, with external defibrillation immediately available, whenever PFA or dual-energy ablation is performed in patients with cardiac devices.

papers.title: First Latin American retrospective registry of cardiac ablation in pediatric and congenital heart disease patients. A LAHRS registry.
papers.journal: Journal of interventional cardiac electrophysiology : an international journal of arrhythmias and pacing
papers.authors: Moltedo JM, Cuesta A, Vidal F, Iturralde P, Márquez-Murillo MF, Levinstein M, et al.
papers.citation: Moltedo JM, Cuesta A, Vidal F, Iturralde P, Márquez-Murillo MF, Levinstein M, et al.. First Latin American retrospective registry of cardiac ablation in pediatric and congenital heart disease patients. A LAHRS registry.. J Interv Card Electrophysiol. 2026 Sep 29;69(6):1529-1536. doi: 10.1007/s10840-026-02442-3 doi.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND:
Catheter ablation has been proven as an effective and safe therapy for tachyarrhythmias in pediatric and congenital heart disease (CHD) patients. Although there are international registries on the use of catheter ablation in these populations, none of them include Latin American countries.

OBJECTIVES:
To assess the clinical characteristics of pediatric and congenital heart disease patients undergoing catheter ablation procedures. Data obtained includes types of arrhythmias, techniques, success, complications and recurrence rates.

MATERIALS AND METHODS:
A descriptive and analytical retrospective observational study was performed. A closed coded online form available for 6 months was used. All electrophysiologists who practice pediatric electrophysiology in Latin America and were identified in a previous LAHSR's survey were invited to participate through Latin American Heart Rhythm Society (LAHRS) electronic media ( https://lahrs.org/ ). Participation was not mandatory, it was not encouraged by any economic or material goods, and an informed consent for the use of the data was required. Consecutive electrophysiological catheter procedures were included in children under 18 years of age or patients with CHD, regardless age, between 2017 and 2021.

RESULTS:
Twenty physicians from 8 Latin American countries participated. A total of 1778 procedures were reported, 53% were male, mean age was 12.4 ± 5.1 years and 8.5% had congenital heart disease. An ablation was attempted in 87% of the patients, using a non-irrigated tip radiofrequency catheter in 68% of them, and a 3-D mapping system in 29%. Radiofrequency was the most commonly used energy source in 98% of the cases. The most frequent substrates were accessory pathways in 69.5% (61% were manifest), followed by AV nodal reentry in 16.5% and ectopic atrial tachycardia in 4%. Additionally, there were 3.8% atrial flutter, 3.8% ventricular tachycardias, 1.2% premature ventricular contractions. Ablation was considered acutely successful in 93% of the cases. Mean total procedural time was 92.1 ± 36.8 min and mean total fluoroscopy time was 16.3 ± 9.4 min. Complication rate was 1.8% and included complete AV block in 3 patients (0.2%). No deaths were reported. The recurrence rate was 8.5%.

CONCLUSIONS:
In this first exclusively pediatric and congenital heart disease retrospective registry of catheter ablation in Latin America, a high rate of success and low incidence of complications was observed. This is in concordance with previously reported registries from other latitudes, proving that ablation is an effective and safe therapy in this group of patients.

papers.title: Catheter ablation of epicardial premature ventricular complexes in patients with and without cardiac scar.
papers.journal: Journal of interventional cardiac electrophysiology : an international journal of arrhythmias and pacing
papers.authors: Jiwani S, Arps K, Shah M, Deshmukh A, Liang JJ, Latchamsetty R, et al.
papers.citation: Jiwani S, Arps K, Shah M, Deshmukh A, Liang JJ, Latchamsetty R, et al.. Catheter ablation of epicardial premature ventricular complexes in patients with and without cardiac scar.. J Interv Card Electrophysiol. 2026 Nov 23;69(8):2491-2497. doi: 10.1007/s10840-026-02351-5 doi.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND:
The left ventricular epicardium is a common site of origin (SOO) among patients with idiopathic premature ventricular complexes (PVCs) undergoing catheter ablation procedures. Less is known about epicardial PVC ablation among patients with myocardial scarring. The objective of this paper is to report on the presence and impact of cardiac scar among patients with epicardial PVCs undergoing ablation procedures.

METHODS:
In a retrospective analysis, patients with epicardial PVCs and late gadolinium enhanced cardiac magnetic resonance (LGE-CMR) imaging were included. Acute and long-term procedural outcomes were examined and stratified by the presence or absence of cardiac scar.

RESULTS:
Twenty-nine patients were included (male 17/29(59%), age 55±14 years, ejection fraction 48±12%, PVC burden 25±12%, ischemic cardiomyopathy (CM) n = 3, non-ischemic CM n = 7, PVC induced CM n = 5). The SOO was left ventricular summit (n = 20), great cardiac vein (n = 2), cardiac crux (n = 4), or basal anterolateral epicardium (n = 3). Ablation within the CVS was limited by proximity to the coronary arteries (n = 16), inaccessibility of ablation catheter (n = 5), or elevated baseline impedance (n = 2). LGE-CMR scar was present at the arrhythmia SOO in 14/29(48%) patients. There were no differences in procedural, radiofrequency, or fluoroscopy times between patients with and without scar (p > 0.05). Ablation was successful in 14/29 patients and partially successful in 8/29 patients; the post-ablation PVC burden was 8±10% with no differences among those with or without cardiac scar (P > 0.05).

CONCLUSION:
Epicardial PVCs may be encountered in patients with and without structural heart disease, with LGE-CMR located at the PVC SOO in almost half of the patients. While LGE-CMR remains a powerful diagnostic modality, its utility in predicting procedural outcomes for epicardial PVC ablation may be limited. Among consecutive patients undergoing ablation of premature ventricular complexes with an epicardial origin, LGE-CMR defined scar was present at the site of origin in approximately 50% of patients.

papers.title: A Single 480-s Cryoablation Reduces Long-Term Arrhythmia Recurrence Rate Than Standard Cryoablation in Patients With AVNRT.
papers.authors: Koca H, Harbalıoğlu H, Ardıc ML, Icen YK, Koca F, Coşkun H, et al.
papers.citation: Koca H, Harbalıoğlu H, Ardıc ML, Icen YK, Koca F, Coşkun H, et al.. A Single 480-s Cryoablation Reduces Long-Term Arrhythmia Recurrence Rate Than Standard Cryoablation in Patients With AVNRT.. J Cardiovasc Electrophysiol. 2026 Apr 28;37(4):714-723. doi: 10.1111/jce.70209 doi.
papers.abstract:
INTRODUCTION:
Focal cryoablation (CRYO) is an alternative to radiofrequency ablation (RFA) in patients with atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT) with low risk of atrioventricular (AV) block and high arrhythmia recurrence. There are limited studies showing that longer duration and bonus CRYO decreases arrhythmia recurrence compared to standard CRYO (two times 240 s). In our study, it was planned to investigate the efficacy of a single 480-s CRYO protocol on the long-term risk of AVNRT recurrence and persistent AV block in AVNRT patients compared to standard CRYO and RFA protocols.

METHODS:
Two hundred sixty patients who underwent ablation for AVNRT were enrolled in this retrospective cohort study. Patients were divided into three groups: standard CRYO group (Group I), single 480-s CRYO group (Group II), and RFA group (Group III). Groups I, II, and III included 92, 68, and 100 AVNRT patients, respectively. Patients were followed for 32 ± 9.1 months after ablation. The groups were compared for acute process success, transient AV block, persistent AV block, and long-term arrhythmic recurrence.

RESULTS:
In the follow-up, AVNRT recurrence was determined in 10, 2, and 3 patients in Groups I, II, and III, respectively (p < 0.001). The frequency of AVNRT recurrence was significantly higher in Group I than in Groups II and III (p < 0.05). It was found that the frequency of AVNRT recurrence was similar between Groups II and III. In Groups I and II, permanent AV block associated with ablation was not observed in either case. However, in Group III, only two patients were found to have permanent AV block. There were no statistical differences between groups in terms of permanent AV block development. Acute process success and transient AV block development were similar among groups.

DISCUSSION:
In our study, it was shown that AVNRT patients can be treated effectively and safely with a single 480-s CRYO protocol among catheter ablation methods. While this new CRYO protocol significantly reduces the long-term arrhythmic recurrence rate compared to standard CRYO, it is similarly effective with RFA.

papers.title: Validation of Cardiorespiratory-Gated Proton Beam Delivery for Stereotactic Arrhythmia Radioablation.
papers.authors: Kang J, Bijari FJ, Chemli Y, Chen YL, Deng H, Depauw N, et al.
papers.citation: Kang J, Bijari FJ, Chemli Y, Chen YL, Deng H, Depauw N, et al.. Validation of Cardiorespiratory-Gated Proton Beam Delivery for Stereotactic Arrhythmia Radioablation.. J Cardiovasc Electrophysiol. 2026 Oct 27;37(10):2375-2384. doi: 10.1111/jce.70512 doi.
papers.abstract:
AIMS:
Stereotactic arrhythmia radioablation (STAR) is a promising noninvasive therapy for refractory ventricular tachycardia. Using scanned proton beams for STAR enables precisely focused, high doses of ionizing radiation. Effective mitigation of target motion is critical for safety but remains challenging due to the complex interplay between beam scanning and cardiorespiratory motion. We evaluated the safety and feasibility of accurately delivering gated scanned proton beams to a ventricular myocardial target and compared lesion outcomes of respiratory (single)- and cardiorespiratory (dual)-gated proton beams.

METHODS:
Six pigs (the first two used as a test of the protocol) underwent baseline CT for treatment planning with a single fractional dose of 35 Gy to a myocardial target in the left ventricular free wall. papers.title: Safety and performance of vibration-assisted extraction of chronic cardiac implantable electronic device leads: A preclinical ovine study.
papers.authors: Ramot Y, Tomer O, Zilberman Barzilai D, Willenz U, Beer O, Tov YS, et al.
papers.citation: Ramot Y, Tomer O, Zilberman Barzilai D, Willenz U, Beer O, Tov YS, et al.. Safety and performance of vibration-assisted extraction of chronic cardiac implantable electronic device leads: A preclinical ovine study.. Heart Rhythm. 2026 Oct 02;23(10):e2343-e2351. doi: 10.1016/j.hrthm.2026.06.042 doi.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND:
Transvenous extraction of chronic cardiac implantable electronic device leads is challenged by fibrotic adhesions and procedural risks. Novel technologies aim to improve safety and efficacy. A high-frequency mechanical vibration system aims to disrupt adhesions.

OBJECTIVE:
This study aimed to evaluate the initial safety, performance, and usability of a novel vibration-assisted lead extraction system in a preclinical Good Laboratory Practice ovine model.

METHODS:
9 leads implanted for >2 years (range 2.9-5.25 years) were extracted from 6 sheep using the vibration system under fluoroscopy. The internal lumen of the leads was used to deliver a customized locking stylet. The stylet was used to deliver vibration energy to the lead, applied for up to 20 minutes/animal. Assessments included procedural success, lead integrity, intraprocedural monitoring, 3-day clinical follow-up, laboratory tests, necropsy, and histopathology (heart, lungs, central veins).

RESULTS:
Procedural success (lead removal) was 100% without adjunctive tools: external cutting sheath was not required for adhesion dissection in all of the cases. Lead release occurred within ∼1 minute in 8 of 9 leads. Primary safety endpoints were met: no central vein or myocardial perforation and no pulmonary embolism. No blood pressure drops, significant arrhythmias, or worsening tricuspid regurgitation occurred. 1 lead fracture (1 of 9) resulted in a retained distal screw (<1 cm) associated with mild localized myocardial necrosis. Anchor device malfunctions required intraprocedural replacement in 2 cases.

CONCLUSION:
Vibration-assisted extraction of chronic cardiac implantable electronic device leads was feasible with a remarkable acute safety profile in this ovine model, meeting primary safety endpoints. The procedure was characterized by notable technical simplicity and rapid lead release via the internal lumen, successfully obviating the requirement for potentially hazardous external cutting sheaths. Lead fracture and anchor malfunctions indicate areas for further technological assessment and clinical trial.

papers.title: Safety, Utility, and Outcomes of Procainamide Challenge for the Diagnosis and Exclusion of Brugada Syndrome.
papers.authors: Moore BM, Chan D, Davies B, Laksman ZWM, Roberts JD, Sanatani S, et al.
papers.citation: Moore BM, Chan D, Davies B, Laksman ZWM, Roberts JD, Sanatani S, et al.. Safety, Utility, and Outcomes of Procainamide Challenge for the Diagnosis and Exclusion of Brugada Syndrome.. Circulation. 2026 Jan 20;153(3):154-163. doi: 10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.125.076011 doi.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND:
The safety, yield, and prognosis of a type 1 procainamide-induced Brugada pattern are incompletely understood and may differ from those of other sodium channel blockers with greater potencies.

METHODS:
The safety of procainamide infusion and yield of a type 1 Brugada pattern were assessed according to indication in consecutive patients from the Canadian Hearts in Rhythm Organization registry. Outcomes were evaluated in patients with a standard or high-lead procainamide-induced Brugada pattern (without previous cardiac arrest) and compared with those with a spontaneous type 1 pattern.

RESULTS:
In 947 consecutive patients undergoing procainamide infusion for the diagnosis or exclusion of Brugada syndrome, 2 patients (0.2%) experienced asymptomatic ventricular arrhythmias related to procainamide, which resolved upon discontinuation of the infusion. The yield of a type 1 pattern was 7.2% in 390 patients with unexplained cardiac arrest, 22.2% in 135 patients with a family history of Brugada syndrome, and 6.9% in 116 patients with a family history of unexplained cardiac arrest or sudden death. Test yield was 46.6% in 189 patients with a non-specific type 2 or 3 Brugada pattern and 92% in those with an intermittent spontaneous type 1 pattern (ie, implied sensitivity of 92%). Estimated specificity was very high. In 137 patients with a procainamide-induced type 1 Brugada pattern (with no previous cardiac arrest) followed for a mean of 5.9±4.5 years, no patients met the primary composite arrhythmic end point (0%). In 105 spontaneous type 1 patients, one patient (1%) met the primary end point after receiving appropriate shocks for ventricular fibrillation. Thirteen percent had a primary prevention implantable cardioverter defibrillator implanted at baseline (one appropriate shock), with an additional 7% undergoing implantable cardioverter defibrillator implantation during follow-up, predominantly for syncope with a suspected arrhythmic mechanism. No patient who underwent implantable cardioverter defibrillator implantation during follow-up subsequently received appropriate therapy.

CONCLUSIONS:
Procainamide infusion is extremely safe for the diagnosis and exclusion of Brugada syndrome, with yield dependent on pretest probability and indication for testing. Estimated sensitivity and specificity appear to be high. Patients with an asymptomatic procainamide-induced type 1 Brugada pattern are at very low risk of malignant ventricular arrhythmias.

papers.title: Atrial fibrillation and flutter conversion with pulsed electric field delivery: preclinical proof of concept.
papers.journal: Journal of interventional cardiac electrophysiology : an international journal of arrhythmias and pacing
papers.authors: Tan NY, Del-Carpio Munoz F, Tri JA, Koya T, Otsuka N, DeSimone CV, et al.
papers.citation: Tan NY, Del-Carpio Munoz F, Tri JA, Koya T, Otsuka N, DeSimone CV, et al.. Atrial fibrillation and flutter conversion with pulsed electric field delivery: preclinical proof of concept.. J Interv Card Electrophysiol. 2026 Oct 14;69(7):1707-1713. doi: 10.1007/s10840-025-02115-7 doi.
papers.abstract:
INTRODUCTION:
Device-based therapies for treating atrial fibrillation (AF) episodes are limited. Using pulsed electric fields (PEF) to induce reversible electroporation of cardiac tissue may effectively terminate AF. Thus, we aimed to assess the feasibility of PEF delivery for converting atrial arrhythmias via reversible electroporation.

METHODS AND RESULTS:
Four swine models were used in this acute study. Custom-made decapolar catheters for PEF delivery were deployed with the following configurations: (1) Endocardial right atrium (RA) and coronary sinus (CS), n = 2; and (2) Endocardial RA and epicardial left atrium (epiLA), n = 2. AF and atrial flutter (AFL) were induced with programmed stimulation. PEF delivery was performed using the BTX 830 generator. For each attempt, a single monophasic pulse at 10 or 20 µs pulse width was administered, with voltage varied across attempts (range 750-3000 V). Successful (type 1 and 2 breaks) and unsuccessful conversion attempts were recorded. Post-PEF signal changes and arrhythmias were identified. A total of 58 AF/AFL (28 and 30 respectively) episodes were induced. Of the 37 successful conversion attempts, 33 (89.1%) were type 1 breaks. Conversion success probabilities generally increased with higher voltages for both configurations. Greater than 70% conversion success was seen with ≥ 1500 V for the RA/CS configuration and ≥ 2000 V for the RA/epiLA configuration. Arrhythmias including intra-atrial delay and high-grade atrioventricular block were seen, usually following successive PEF deliveries. Significant muscle stimulation was provoked with the current experimental setup.

CONCLUSION:
Termination of atrial arrhythmias with PEF delivery is feasible, although further work is required to optimize its efficacy and safety.

papers.title: Ventricular nanosecond pulsed electric field delivery using active fixation leads: a proof-of-concept preclinical study.
papers.journal: Journal of interventional cardiac electrophysiology : an international journal of arrhythmias and pacing
papers.authors: Tan NY, Ladas TP, Christopoulos G, Sugrue AM, van Zyl M, Ladejobi AO, et al.
papers.citation: Tan NY, Ladas TP, Christopoulos G, Sugrue AM, van Zyl M, Ladejobi AO, et al.. Ventricular nanosecond pulsed electric field delivery using active fixation leads: a proof-of-concept preclinical study.. J Interv Card Electrophysiol. 2026 Oct 30;69(7):1617-1627. doi: 10.1007/s10840-022-01268-z doi.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND:
Mid-myocardial ventricular arrhythmias are challenging to treat. Cardiac electroporation via pulsed electric fields (PEFs) offers significant promise. We therefore tested PEF delivery using screw-in pacemaker leads as proof-of-concept.

METHODS:
In 5 canine models, we applied nanosecond PEF (pulse width 300 ns) across the right ventricular (RV) septum using a single lead bipolar configuration (n = 2) and between two leads (n = 3). We recorded electrograms (EGMs) prior to, immediately post, and 5 min after PEF. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (cMRI) and histopathology were performed at 2 weeks and 1 month.

RESULTS:
Nanosecond PEF induced minimal extracardiac stimulation and frequent ventricular ectopy that terminated post-treatment; no canines died with PEF delivery. With 1 lead, energy delivery ranged from 0.64 to 7.28 J. Transient ST elevations were seen post-PEF. No myocardial delayed enhancement (MDE) was seen on cMRI. No lesions were noted on the RV septum at autopsy. With 2 leads, energy delivery ranged from 56.3 to 144.9 J. Persistent ST elevations and marked EGM amplitude decreases developed post-PEF. MDE was seen along the septum 2 weeks and 1 month post-PEF. There were discrete fibrotic lesions along the septum; pathology revealed dense connective tissue with < 5% residual cardiomyocytes.

CONCLUSIONS:
Ventricular electroporation is feasible and safe with an active fixation device. Reversible changes were seen with lower energy PEF delivery, whereas durable lesions were created at higher energies.

papers.title: Feasibility, Safety, and Efficacy of Pulsed Field Ablation for Ventricular Arrhythmias: Insights From a Large Health System Registry in the United States.
papers.authors: Prasitlumkum N, Rodriguez-Riascos JF, Vemulapalli H, Somappa A, Estrada-Vargas CA, Fatunde OA, et al.
papers.citation: Prasitlumkum N, Rodriguez-Riascos JF, Vemulapalli H, Somappa A, Estrada-Vargas CA, Fatunde OA, et al.. Feasibility, Safety, and Efficacy of Pulsed Field Ablation for Ventricular Arrhythmias: Insights From a Large Health System Registry in the United States.. J Cardiovasc Electrophysiol. 2026 Sep 15;:. doi: 10.1111/jce.70503 doi.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND:
Pulsed field ablation (PFA) is an emerging non-thermal ablation modality with proven safety in atrial arrhythmia ablation. However, data on its performance for ventricular arrhythmias (VA) remain limited.

OBJECTIVE:
To evaluate the feasibility, safety, and efficacy of PFA for complex VA in a multicenter real-world US registry.

METHODS:
This retrospective study included consecutive patients undergoing PFA for ventricular tachycardia (VT) or premature ventricular contractions (PVCs) at three Mayo Clinic centers (April 2024 to July 2025). The primary feasibility outcome was the successful delivery of PFA lesions to the intended target substrate. Primary efficacy outcomes included acute procedural success; sustained VT recurrence requiring implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) shocks or multiple antitachycardia pacing therapies; and ≥ 80% reduction in PVC burden. Safety outcomes included procedural complications, valvular function, thromboembolic events, renal function, and conduction disturbances.

RESULTS:
Twenty-six patients were included (13 PVC, 13 VT). Acute success was achieved in all VT ablations (69.2% complete; 30.8% partial) and in 92.3% of PVC ablations. Complications occurred in 11.5% of patients (transient LBBB [n = 1] and vascular complications [n = 2]). No thromboembolic events, intracardiac thrombus, or acute kidney injury were observed. Lesions near the mitral valve apparatus did not worsen mitral regurgitation, including in patients with pre-existing valve disease. After a median follow-up of 365 days, one patient experienced VT recurrence requiring ICD shocks. Estimated recurrence-free survival after VT ablation was 61.5% at 12 months; 58.3% of PVC patients achieved ≥ 80% burden reduction.

CONCLUSION:
PFA for VA appears feasible and acutely effective, with a low rate of procedure-related complications. While acute success was high, long-term outcomes were acceptable for VT ablation and relatively modest for PVC ablation, highlighting the need for continued refinement of technology and energy-delivery strategies. Larger prospective studies are warranted.

PFA for VA appears feasible and acutely effective, with a low rate of procedure-related complications.  While acute success was high, long-term outcomes were acceptable for VT ablation and relatively modest for PVC ablation, highlighting the need for continued refinement of technology and energy-delivery strategies. papers.title: Preventive Linear Ablation Strategy for Intra-Atrial Reentrant Tachycardia Following Cardiac Surgery.
papers.authors: Chen J, Pan T, Liu Y, Chen Z, Zhao Y, Bai J, et al.
papers.citation: Chen J, Pan T, Liu Y, Chen Z, Zhao Y, Bai J, et al.. Preventive Linear Ablation Strategy for Intra-Atrial Reentrant Tachycardia Following Cardiac Surgery.. J Arrhythm. 2026 Dec 09;42(6):e70508. doi: 10.1002/joa3.70508 doi.
papers.abstract:
AIMS:
Intra-atrial reentrant tachycardia (IART) frequently occurs following cardiac surgery due to scar-related conduction abnormalities. While advances in mapping technologies have improved the acute success rate of catheter ablation, arrhythmia recurrence remains a significant clinical concern. This study aimed to evaluate whether a preventive linear ablation strategy guided by voltage mapping improves the long-term success rate of catheter ablation in patients with IART post-cardiac surgery.

METHODS AND RESULTS:
A total of 46 consecutive patients following cardiac surgery who underwent atrial tachycardia ablation between 2022 and 2024 were enrolled in the study group. After activation mapping-guided ablation for ongoing IART, preventive linear ablation was performed based on voltage mapping. Fifty consecutive sex- and age-matched patients with cardiac surgery undergoing activation mapping-guided ablation alone served as the historical control group between 2018 and 2021. At a mean follow-up of 21 ± 4.9 months, the rate of freedom from atrial arrhythmias was significantly higher in the study group compared to the control group (82.6% vs. 64.0%; = 0.019). Despite the improved outcomes, the study group had significantly longer total procedure times (192 ± 37 vs. 126 ± 25 min; < 0.001) and radiofrequency ablation durations (29 ± 5 vs. 20 ± 6 min; < 0.001). However, there were no significant differences in complication rates between the two groups.

CONCLUSIONS:
Preventive linear ablation strategy was associated with improved arrhythmia-free survival in patients with IART post cardiac surgery, but these exploratory findings require confirmation in future prospective studies.

papers.title: Deep Sedation in Single-Shot Pulmonary Vein Isolation: A Head-to-Head Look at Two Pulsed Field Versus Cryoballoon Ablation Approaches.
papers.authors: Kheir JA, Schaack D, Urbani A, Urbanek L, Marx A, Lurz J, et al.
papers.citation: Kheir JA, Schaack D, Urbani A, Urbanek L, Marx A, Lurz J, et al.. Deep Sedation in Single-Shot Pulmonary Vein Isolation: A Head-to-Head Look at Two Pulsed Field Versus Cryoballoon Ablation Approaches.. J Cardiovasc Electrophysiol. 2026 Nov 09;:. doi: 10.1111/jce.70554 doi.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND:
Deep sedation (DS) is routinely used during single-shot pulmonary vein isolation (PVI) to optimize patient comfort and procedural stability. However, data on sedative requirements and procedural tolerance of pulsed field ablation (PFA) under DS compared with thermal technologies remain limited.

METHODS:
In this single-center study, consecutive patients underwent PVI with cryoballoon (CB), PFA using a pentaspline catheter (PC) or the balloon-in-basket catheter (BC). All procedures were performed under DS with midazolam, fentanyl, and propofol, administered by electrophysiology staff without anaesthesiologist supervision. Propensity score matching (1:1:1) was applied for age, sex, body mass index, and hypertension. Procedural characteristics, sedative/analgesic requirements, and complications were analyzed.

RESULTS:
Acute PVI without major complications was achieved in all 156 enrolled patients. PC procedures were associated with higher body-weight- and time-adjusted requirements for propofol (CB: 0.10 ± 0.04 mg/kg/min; PC: 0.15 ± 0.04 mg/kg/min; BC: 0.11 ± 0.03 mg/kg/min; p < 0.001) despite the lowest total dose of propofol used (CB: 440 ± 144 mg; PC: 348± 80 mg; BC: 433 ± 160 mg; p = 0.00). Procedural times (CB: 47.5 [40-60] min, PC: 29 [25-35] min, BC: 47.5 [40-56] min, p < 0.001) and fluoroscopy times (CB: 9.5 [6.3-13.6] min; PC: 6.2 [4.4-9] min; BC: 7.2 [6.1-11.2] min, p = 0.001) were shortest in the PC group. Sedation-related hemodynamic stability was comparable across all cohorts.

CONCLUSIONS:
The novel BC demonstrated excellent feasibility under DS, with reduced normalized sedative requirements compared with the PC and a safety profile comparable to CB ablation. These findings suggest that optimized waveform design and field homogeneity may enable safe and comfortable PVI under DS without the need for general anesthesia.

papers.title: Cardiac electrophysiology procedures must be performed exclusively by trained electrophysiologists: A statement from the Heart Rhythm Society and Heart Rhythm Advocates.
papers.authors: Greenberg SJ, Chung MK, Lakkireddy D, Al-Khatib SM, Aryana A, Di Biase L, et al.
papers.citation: Greenberg SJ, Chung MK, Lakkireddy D, Al-Khatib SM, Aryana A, Di Biase L, et al.. Cardiac electrophysiology procedures must be performed exclusively by trained electrophysiologists: A statement from the Heart Rhythm Society and Heart Rhythm Advocates.. Heart Rhythm. 2026 Nov 06;:. doi: 10.1016/j.hrthm.2026.09.046 doi.
papers.abstract: The exponential growth of clinical cardiac electrophysiology (CCEP) as a subspecialty has created an important unresolved question in contemporary cardiovascular medicine: Who is qualified to perform electrophysiology (EP) procedures? As nonelectrophysiologists increasingly perform procedures that require the nuanced expertise of a trained or board-certified CCEP (eg, permanent pacemaker implantation, implantable cardioverter-defibrillator implantation, cardiac resynchronization therapy, and transvenous lead extraction), the consequences for patient safety, procedural outcomes, and health system efficiency have become impossible to ignore. This article presents a comprehensive, evidence-based argument that cardiac EP procedures must be performed exclusively by physicians who have completed accredited fellowship training in CCEP. We draw upon peer-reviewed outcome data, guideline-derived training standards from the Heart Rhythm Society, the American College of Cardiology, and American Heart Association, including the newly published 2026 American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association/Heart Rhythm Society Advanced Training Statement on Clinical Cardiac Electrophysiology, as well as registry analyses spanning hundreds of thousands of patients to substantiate our position. The risks associated with suboptimal operator training are not theoretical; they are measurable, costly, and potentially fatal. The evidence presented demonstrates that operator specialization in EP is among the most powerful independent predictors of procedural safety and long-term outcomes and can be as important as institutional volume in many analyses. We call upon hospital credentialing committees, national medical societies, payers, regulatory bodies, and policymakers worldwide to establish and enforce a definitive standard: only trained CCEPs should implant and manage cardiac implantable electronic devices, perform catheter ablation procedures, execute transvenous lead extraction, and conduct formal EP studies.

papers.title: Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease and Sudden Cardiac Death: Epidemiology, Mechanisms, Risk Stratification, and Prevention.
papers.authors: Liu ZY, Qin ZH, Liu YF, Wei HT, Zhang RY
papers.citation: Liu ZY, Qin ZH, Liu YF, Wei HT, Zhang RY. Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease and Sudden Cardiac Death: Epidemiology, Mechanisms, Risk Stratification, and Prevention.. Heart Rhythm. 2026 Nov 06;:. doi: 10.1016/j.hrthm.2026.10.066 doi.
papers.abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) has emerged as the most prevalent chronic metabolic liver disease worldwide. Cardiovascular adverse events have long been the leading cause of death in the MASLD population, far exceeding liver-related mortality. Sudden cardiac death (SCD) represents the most insidious and rapidly progressing extreme clinical phenotype among these cardiovascular complications. However, the relationship between MASLD and SCD has long received insufficient attention. Accumulating evidence from clinical studies indicates that MASLD is associated with elevated sudden cardiac arrest (SCA) risk independent of conventional cardiometabolic risk factors. Notably, while non-invasive clinical proxies of hepatic steatosis (such as the fatty liver index) identify individuals with heightened susceptibility to SCA, advancing liver fibrosis shows the strongest, gradient-dependent association with adverse cardiovascular outcomes, although its relation to SCA or SCD specifically requires confirmation. Sudden death in MASLD may result from primary ventricular arrhythmias or, in advanced cirrhosis, from non-shockable arrest due to hemodynamic, infectious, or metabolic decompensation. Although shared cardiometabolic risk factors account for a substantial portion of this association, proposed mechanisms include insulin resistance-related myocardial energy disturbances, inflammation-associated myocardial and electrophysiological remodeling, cirrhosis-associated circulatory dysfunction, and gut-derived endotoxemia. In clinical practice, non-invasive fibrosis scores, circulating biomarkers, and imaging parameters represent promising candidate risk markers for evaluating electrophysiological vulnerability, though a validated, MASLD-specific SCD risk prediction model remains to be established. Strategies such as lifestyle intervention, metabolic-targeted pharmacotherapy, and intensive management of cardiovascular risk factors may interrupt the progression from MASLD to SCD. This review summarizes the current evidence to inform cardiovascular risk management across the course of MASLD.

papers.title: Electrocardiographic and Echocardiographic Markers of Atrial and Ventricular Remodeling Allow Identification of Cardiac Sarcoidosis.
papers.authors: Kuss PC, Frye BC, Fähndrich S, Dvorak I, Westermann D, Lehrmann H, et al.
papers.citation: Kuss PC, Frye BC, Fähndrich S, Dvorak I, Westermann D, Lehrmann H, et al.. Electrocardiographic and Echocardiographic Markers of Atrial and Ventricular Remodeling Allow Identification of Cardiac Sarcoidosis.. JACC Clin Electrophysiol. 2026 Nov 05;:. doi: 10.1016/j.jacep.2026.10.001 doi.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND:
Cardiac sarcoidosis (CS) is a rare but life-threatening manifestation of systemic sarcoidosis. Although positron emission tomography-computed tomography (PET-CT) and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging provide high diagnostic accuracy, they are unsuitable for first-line screening. Widely available modalities such as electrocardiography (ECG) and transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) focusing only on ventricular abnormalities show limited sensitivity.

OBJECTIVES:
This study aims to evaluate whether a combined diagnostic model integrating ECG and TTE parameters, emphasizing atrial and ventricular remodeling, can accurately identify patients with CS.

METHODS:
We prospectively included 252 consecutive patients with biopsy-proven sarcoidosis. CS was defined by characteristic findings on PET-CT or cardiac magnetic resonance imaging. A comprehensive set of atrial and ventricular ECG and TTE parameters was analyzed. Diagnostic models were constructed using univariable and multivariable logistic regression, and discriminative performance was assessed.

RESULTS:
CS was identified in 37 (14.7%) patients. On ECG, prolonged P-wave duration, prolonged QRS duration, and reduced T-wave amplitude in lead aVR were independently associated with CS. On TTE, increased left atrial volume index, increased left ventricular end-diastolic diameter, and impaired left ventricular global longitudinal strain emerged as significant predictors. ECG- and TTE-based models showed comparable discrimination for CS identification (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve: 0.87 for both). A combined ECG/TTE model, driven primarily by QRS duration, left atrial volume index, and left ventricular global longitudinal strain, achieved the highest diagnostic performance (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve: 0.90).

CONCLUSIONS:
An exploratory multimodal, noninvasive approach integrating atrial and ventricular ECG and TTE markers provides high diagnostic accuracy for identifying CS and may serve as a pragmatic screening and triage tool to guide referral for advanced cardiac imaging. papers.title: Beyond anticoagulation: defining the role of left atrial appendage closure in stroke prevention for atrial fibrillation.
papers.journal: Europace : European pacing, arrhythmias, and cardiac electrophysiology : journal of the working groups on cardiac pacing, arrhythmias, and cardiac cellular electrophysiology of the European Society of Cardiology
papers.authors: Camm AJ
papers.citation: Camm AJ. Beyond anticoagulation: defining the role of left atrial appendage closure in stroke prevention for atrial fibrillation.. Europace. 2026 Nov 04;28(11):. doi: 10.1093/europace/euag296 doi.
papers.abstract: Oral anticoagulation has a very strong evidence base for stroke prevention in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) at elevated thromboembolic risk. Direct oral anticoagulants have improved the safety and convenience of treatment, yet important limitations remain, including residual ischaemic stroke, major bleeding, treatment discontinuation, and patient refusal. Left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) offers an alternative strategy for selected patients by excluding the principal anatomical source of AF-related cardiac thrombi. However, the appropriate role of LAAC remains controversial, particularly in patients who can and do tolerate anticoagulation. This viewpoint argues for a more individualized approach that distinguishes absolute contraindications from modifiable bleeding risks, treatment refusal or non-persistence, and stroke occurring despite adequate anticoagulation.

papers.authors: Antoniou CK, Tsiachris D, Karanikola AE, Botis M, Kordalis A, Doundoulakis I, et al.
papers.citation: Antoniou CK, Tsiachris D, Karanikola AE, Botis M, Kordalis A, Doundoulakis I, et al.. J Arrhythm. 2026 Dec 05;42(6):e70520. doi: 10.1002/joa3.70520 doi.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND:
Acute effects of pulsed field ablation (PFA) on passive atrial mechanical properties have not hitherto been assessed by reconstruction of pressure-volume relationship using invasive intracavitary pressure measurements.

METHODS:
In a cohort of 38 first-time atrial fibrillation ablation patients, submitted to pulmonary vein isolation, we studied the effects of PFA and cryoballoon ablation on the left atrial elastic constant and passive elastic chamber stiffness constant, expressing baseline left atrial conditions and quantifying passive left atrial stiffness, respectively. Left atrial pressure was invasively measured immediately pre- and post-procedurally, while volume values were obtained echocardiographically.

RESULTS:
No differences were noted in passive elastic chamber stiffness constant values, pre- and post-procedurally in either group. No differences were noted between CBA and PFA groups. There were no observable associations between Δ and Δ and either AF duration or preprocedural left atrial volume.

CONCLUSIONS:
Based on the above, CBA and PFA demonstrated comparable effects on left atrial mechanical properties in the acute post-ablation setting.

papers.abstractJa:
【背景】

Acute effects of pulsed field ablation (PFA) on passive atrial mechanical properties have not hitherto been assessed by reconstruction of pressure-volume relationship using invasive intracavitary pressure measurements.

METHODS:
In a cohort of 38 first-time atrial fibrillation ablation patients, submitted to pulmonary vein isolation, we studied the effects of PFA and cryoballoon ablation on the left atrial elastic constant and passive elastic chamber stiffness constant, expressing baseline left atrial conditions and quantifying passive left atrial stiffness, respectively.
Left atrial pressure was invasively measured immediately pre- and post-procedurally, while volume values were obtained echocardiographically.

RESULTS:
No differences were noted in passive elastic chamber stiffness constant values, pre- and post-procedurally in either group.  No differences were noted between CBA and PFA groups.  There were no observable associations between Δ and Δ and either AF duration or preprocedural left atrial volume.

CONCLUSIONS:
Based on the above, CBA and PFA demonstrated comparable effects on left atrial mechanical properties in the acute post-ablation setting.

papers.title: Tailor-Made Hybrid Pulsed-Field and Radiofrequency Ablation Guided by ExTRa Mapping for Refractory Long-Standing Persistent Atrial Fibrillation: First Experience With the Affera System Prism-2.
papers.authors: Kawaji T, Naka M, Okubo S, Ishida R, Ashihara T
papers.citation: Kawaji T, Naka M, Okubo S, Ishida R, Ashihara T. Tailor-Made Hybrid Pulsed-Field and Radiofrequency Ablation Guided by ExTRa Mapping for Refractory Long-Standing Persistent Atrial Fibrillation: First Experience With the Affera System Prism-2.. J Arrhythm. 2026 Dec 04;42(6):e70519. doi: 10.1002/joa3.70519 doi.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND:
Pulmonary vein isolation (PVI) alone is frequently insufficient for persistent atrial fibrillation (AF). Although pulsed-field ablation (PFA) ensures durable linear lesions, extensive transmural ablation risks iatrogenic atrial tachycardia. A tailored strategy combining PFA with titrated radiofrequency (RF) energy for mild substrate homogenization remains poorly defined.

CASE SUMMARY:
A 77-year-old male with post-stroke refractory long-standing AF underwent a re-do ablation. Biatrial substrate evaluation was performed using the ExTRa mapping system, enabled by the Affera system (Prism-2) to visualize the nonmagnetic 20-pole spiral catheter. Areas with a mean non-passively activated ratio (%NP) ≥ 35% and low voltage (< 0.3 mV) were targeted. Following PFA-led posterior wall isolation, mild homogenization was performed using the Sphere-9 catheter with highly titrated RF energy (60%, 60°C, and 1-s duration). Although AF did not terminate directly, the AF cycle length significantly prolonged, and sinus rhythm was restored via cardioversion. Post-procedural mapping confirmed complete isolation without extensive dense scar formation at homogenization sites. The patient maintained sinus rhythm during follow-up.

CONCLUSION:
The hybrid PFA/RF system integrated with AI-driven phase mapping enables a safe, non-destructive, tailor-made substrate modification strategy for refractory persistent AF.

papers.title: The Art Behind the Algorithm: Hybrid Ablation and the Need for a Lifetime Strategy in Non-Paroxysmal Atrial Fibrillation.
papers.journal: Europace : European pacing, arrhythmias, and cardiac electrophysiology : journal of the working groups on cardiac pacing, arrhythmias, and cardiac cellular electrophysiology of the European Society of Cardiology
papers.authors: Spadaccio C, Schena S, Sherman AJ
papers.citation: Spadaccio C, Schena S, Sherman AJ. The Art Behind the Algorithm: Hybrid Ablation and the Need for a Lifetime Strategy in Non-Paroxysmal Atrial Fibrillation.. Europace. 2026 Nov 06;:. doi: 10.1093/europace/euag306 doi.
papers.abstract: The management of persistent and long-standing persistent atrial fibrillation remains highly variable in clinical practice, despite increasingly refined guidelines and an expanding ablation armamentarium. Treatment sequencing is frequently driven by local program infrastructure and institutional culture, and hybrid ablation is often deferred until multiple endocardial procedures have failed, by which point progressive atrial remodeling may have already narrowed the therapeutic window. Randomized and registry data support a meaningful role for hybrid ablation earlier in the disease course of selected patients with non-paroxysmal AF, particularly those with enlarged atria, prolonged AF duration, advanced substrate, or failed prior endocardial ablation. Contemporary pulsed-field ablation technology has improved procedural safety and efficiency, yet freedom from recurrence at one year in persistent AF remains substantially lower than in paroxysmal AF across all current energy platforms, reflecting the complexity of atrial substrate over time. This ongoing myocardial remodeling places non-paroxysmal AF closer to a chronic structural cardiac disease than to a discrete procedural target and demands a lifetime management strategy rather than a sequence of isolated procedural decisions. The mindset for other progressive structural cardiac diseases has already moved in this direction-aortic valve stenosis is now managed through a multidisciplinary team that integrates anatomy, timing, procedural durability, and long-term risk across the full patient trajectory. We propose an AF Heart Team framework for non-paroxysmal AF in which catheter-based, hybrid, and surgical strategies are selected according to disease phenotype and lifetime trajectory, with the goal of intervening before advanced remodeling reduces the likelihood of durable rhythm control.

papers.title: Microgravity and Cardiac Electrophysiology: Autonomic Remodeling, Arrhythmogenesis, and Implications for Long-Duration Spaceflight.
papers.authors: Ciaccio EJ, Talke M, Peters NS, Schwartz SM, Coromilas J, Yarmohammadi H, et al.
papers.citation: Ciaccio EJ, Talke M, Peters NS, Schwartz SM, Coromilas J, Yarmohammadi H, et al.. Microgravity and Cardiac Electrophysiology: Autonomic Remodeling, Arrhythmogenesis, and Implications for Long-Duration Spaceflight.. Heart Rhythm. 2026 Nov 04;:. doi: 10.1016/j.hrthm.2026.10.065 doi.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND:
In microgravity, the human heart undergoes significant geometric and functional remodeling due to the removal of gravity-dependent hydrostatic gradients. These adaptations include a transition from an elliptical to a more spherical shape configuration. Furthermore, cephalad fluid shifts trigger an early spaceflight diuresis, inducing a stable reduction in circulating plasma volume.

OBJECTIVE:
To describe resulting electrophysiologic alterations and arrhythmia promotion.

METHOD:
While most spaceflight arrhythmias are transient and non-lethal, they remain a concern for long-duration missions. Frequently reported irregularities include isolated premature atrial and ventricular complexes. Other events, including non-sustained ventricular tachycardia during spaceflight, the possibility of early-onset atrial fibrillation, and atherosclerosis in former astronauts following exposure to high-energy ionizing radiation have been documented, though the association is still being evaluated. The underlying arrhythmogenic substrate is driven by autonomic resetting, spatiotemporal heterogeneity, and QTc interval prolongation.

RESULTS:
The National Aeronautics and Space Administration utilizes a multi-faceted approach to maintain electrical stability, incorporating high-intensity interval training and electrolyte monitoring and supplementation. Real-time monitoring of wearable technology enables continuous telemetry of the heart. Recently, automated chest compression devices have been shown to significantly outperform manual cardiopulmonary resuscitation in microgravity environments.

CONCLUSION:
Although structural changes typically revert to baseline upon return to Earth gravity, deep-space missions present some risks. Astronauts exposed to ionizing radiation beyond Earth's magnetic field may face risk of long-term cardiovascular disease. Design of personalized nutrition to mitigate electrolyte loss and development of advanced screening tools for cardiac risk assessment are essential to improve the safety of future planetary missions.

papers.title: Controversy: Anticoagulants need to be maintained after catheter ablation of atrial fibrillation in patients at risk of stroke-Pro and Contra.
papers.journal: Europace : European pacing, arrhythmias, and cardiac electrophysiology : journal of the working groups on cardiac pacing, arrhythmias, and cardiac cellular electrophysiology of the European Society of Cardiology
papers.authors: Boriani G, Boveda S, Mei DA, Fauchier L, Imberti JF, Providencia R, et al.
papers.citation: Boriani G, Boveda S, Mei DA, Fauchier L, Imberti JF, Providencia R, et al.. Controversy: Anticoagulants need to be maintained after catheter ablation of atrial fibrillation in patients at risk of stroke-Pro and Contra.. Europace. 2026 Nov 02;:. doi: 10.1093/europace/euag311 doi.
papers.abstract:
The pillars of atrial fibrillation (AF) management include stroke prevention, patient-centred symptom directed decisions on rhythm or rate control, and the proactive management of comorbidities and lifestyle changes. These pillars are not in isolation; they are complementary to each other. While oral anticoagulants (OACs) are highly effective for reducing stroke and all-cause mortality in patients with AF, these drugs confer a risk of major bleeding, including intracranial bleeding. Evidence from clinical trials and observational data shows that early rhythm control, especially with catheter ablation, 

RESULTS:
in a reduction in stroke risk and/or the reduction in AF burden. The question arises therefore, whether in patients with intermediate or low stroke risk after successful catheter ablation, whether or not to continue or discontinue OAC. Recent randomized trials and observational data have created some debate about whether OAC can be routinely stopped after a successful catheter ablation procedure, without a higher risk of thromboembolism. In this pro/contra article, we will debate the arguments for and against the cessation of anti-coagulation after catheter ablation, in the context of recent evidence from clinical trials, observational data, and meta-analysis.

papers.title: Whole-Exome Sequencing Identifies a Rare CSRP3 Variant Associated With Familial Brugada Syndrome in a Lebanese Family.
papers.authors: Bashir Z, Kadhi A, Ballout J, Samara B, Khoury M, Nemer G, et al.
papers.citation: Bashir Z, Kadhi A, Ballout J, Samara B, Khoury M, Nemer G, et al.. Whole-Exome Sequencing Identifies a Rare CSRP3 Variant Associated With Familial Brugada Syndrome in a Lebanese Family.. J Cardiovasc Electrophysiol. 2026 Oct 29;:. doi: 10.1111/jce.70546 doi.
papers.abstract:
INTRODUCTION:
Brugada syndrome (BrS) is an inherited arrhythmia associated with an increased risk of sudden cardiac death. Although traditionally regarded as a primary cardiac channelopathy, pathogenic variants in SCN5A account for only 20%-30% of clinically diagnosed cases, leaving most patients genetically unresolved. Emerging evidence suggests that structural cardiac genes may also contribute to BrS susceptibility. We investigated the genetic basis of BrS in a consanguineous Lebanese family with three affected brothers.

METHODS AND RESULTS:
Whole-exome sequencing was performed in all affected individuals, followed by variant calling, annotation, and phenotype-driven prioritization using Franklin (Genoox). Candidate variants were evaluated according to allele frequency, inheritance model, segregation, and ACMG/AMP classification. Evolutionary conservation, AlphaMissense prediction, protein domain annotation, and structural modeling were performed to assess the potential functional impact of the prioritized variant. Whole-exome sequencing identified a rare homozygous CSRP3 missense variant (NM_003476.5:c.56 A > G; p.His19Arg) shared by all three affected siblings. Following exome-wide filtering under a recessive inheritance model, CSRP3 represented the only rare homozygous coding variant, while no pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants were identified in established Brugada syndrome-associated genes. The variant was absent from public population databases and an internal cohort of Lebanese exomes. His19 was highly conserved across vertebrate species, AlphaMissense classified the variant as likely pathogenic (score = 0.942), and structural modeling predicted alterations within the N-terminal LIM domain that may affect protein stability and local residue interactions.

CONCLUSIONS:
Our findings nominate CSRP3 as a candidate susceptibility gene for Brugada syndrome and support the emerging role of structural cardiac genes in inherited arrhythmia syndromes. Although functional validation is required to establish causality, this study highlights the value of whole-exome sequencing in consanguineous and underrepresented populations for identifying rare candidate variants contributing to BrS susceptibility.

papers.title: Posterior Pulmonary Vein Isolation Lesion Spacing and Left Atrial Posterior Wall Narrowing During Pulsed Field Ablation.
papers.authors: Saito Y, Nagashima K, Watanabe R, Otsuka N, Hirata S, Hirata M, et al.
papers.citation: Saito Y, Nagashima K, Watanabe R, Otsuka N, Hirata S, Hirata M, et al.. Posterior Pulmonary Vein Isolation Lesion Spacing and Left Atrial Posterior Wall Narrowing During Pulsed Field Ablation.. J Arrhythm. 2026 Dec 28;42(6):e70509. doi: 10.1002/joa3.70509 doi.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND:
Left atrial posterior wall (LAPW) narrowing after excessive extension of bilateral pulmonary vein isolation (PVI) lines during pulsed field ablation (PFA) may create a proarrhythmic substrate. The CARTO 3-integrated variable-loop circular catheter (VLCC) provides real-time tissue proximity indication (TPI) and ablation-tag location, but their relationship with LAPW narrowing remains unclear. Therefore, we evaluated associations of TPI status and inter-tag distance (ITD) with acute LAPW narrowing and whether an ITD-guided workflow was associated with LAPW preservation.

METHODS:
Fifty-two retrospective and 27 prospective atrial fibrillation patients underwent PFA using a VLCC. In the retrospective phase, we evaluated the association between ITD, measured using TPI-positive tags and all tags, and LAPW narrowing (< 10 mm) and derived a cutoff. In the prospective phase, the ITD-guided workflow was applied, and we assessed residual LAPW band width.

RESULTS:
In the retrospective phase, both TPI-positive-tag ITD and all-tag ITD correlated with LAPW band width ( = 0.63 and 0.70, respectively; both < 0.001). All-tag ITD showed a numerically higher AUC for LAPW narrowing than TPI-positive-tag ITD (0.869 vs. 0.795; = 0.099), with an optimal all-tag ITD cutoff of 16.5 mm. In the prospective phase incorporating the all-tag ITD cutoff, residual LAPW band widths were wider at the roof (19.4 ± 7.9 vs. 25.1 ± 7.1 mm; = 0.002) and carina (13.6 ± 7.1 vs. 20.8 ± 8.0 mm; < 0.001) than in the retrospective phase.

CONCLUSIONS:
An all-tag ITD-guided workflow was associated with greater preservation of the residual LAPW band width.
